steps.body: You already know halves (2 equal parts) and fourths (4 equal parts). **Thirds** are a new share: splitting a whole into 3 equal parts.

widget.prompt: Show one third of the bar.
widget.successFeedback: One of three equal pieces. The bottom number tells you HOW MANY pieces the whole was cut into — and the more pieces, the smaller each one gets.
widget.lowFeedback: That is less than a third of the bar.
widget.highFeedback: That is more than a third of the bar.

predict.prompt: The bar starts at 1/2. Before you touch it: is 1/2 more or less of the bar than 1/3?
predict.reveal: With the same whole, the bar settles it: 1/2 covers more than 1/3. Count of pieces and size of pieces work together — neither alone decides the amount.

cml.actionGoal: Manipulate the model and track how it represents ssg2 thirds count.
invariants: The manipulated model and the mathematical relationship for ssg2 thirds count must stay consistent.
misconceptions: Changing a visible feature without preserving the relationship that defines ssg2 thirds count.
cml.counterfactualPrompt: What change would make the model stop representing the same mathematical relationship?

widget.prompt: If a whole is split into thirds, how many equal parts are there?

commonErrors.feedback: That's halves. Thirds is 3 equal parts.
Splitting means more than 1 piece. Thirds is 3 equal parts.

steps.body: Just like halves and fourths, thirds must be truly EQUAL in size — 3 pieces of different sizes aren't thirds, no matter how many pieces there are.

widget.prompt: A shape is cut into 3 pieces, but one is bigger than the others. Are these thirds?

options.label: No — thirds must be three equal pieces
options.feedback: Yes — thirds require 3 EQUAL pieces, and these aren't equal.

options.label: Yes — there are 3 pieces
options.feedback: Having 3 pieces isn't enough — they must be equal in size to be thirds.

options.label: Yes, close enough
options.feedback: Thirds must be exactly equal, not just close in size.

steps.body: You can split into thirds in different directions — straight cuts, or from the center — as long as all 3 pieces cover the same amount.

widget.prompt: A rectangle is split into thirds. How many equal pieces are there?

commonErrors.feedback: That's fourths. Thirds is 3 equal pieces.
That's halves. Thirds is 3 equal pieces.

explanationVariants: A circle split into thirds still means 3 equal parts.
Any shape split into thirds gives 3 equal pieces.

widget.prompt: A circle is split into thirds. How many equal pieces are there?

commonErrors.feedback: That's halves. Thirds is 3 equal pieces.
That's fourths. Thirds is 3 equal pieces.

explanationVariants: Unequal pieces are never thirds, no matter how many there are.
For thirds, all 3 pieces must be the exact same size.

widget.prompt: A circle is cut into 3 pieces of different sizes. Are these thirds?

options.label: No — the pieces aren't equal
options.feedback: Yes — thirds must be equal in size, and these pieces aren't.

options.label: Yes, there are 3 pieces
options.feedback: Having 3 pieces isn't enough — the pieces must be equal to be thirds.

options.label: Yes, if you call them thirds
options.feedback: You can't call unequal pieces thirds just by naming them that. They must be equal.

widget.prompt: If you split a whole into thirds, how many equal parts do you get?

commonErrors.feedback: 2 would be halves. Thirds means 3 equal parts.
6 equal parts would be sixths, not thirds. Thirds is 3.

hints: "Third" means one of three equal parts.
So splitting into thirds makes 3 parts.

steps.body: Thirds are 3 equal parts of a whole — a new share alongside halves and fourths.
takeaways: Thirds means splitting into 3 equal parts.
The 3 pieces must be truly equal in size.
Any shape can be split into thirds, in different ways.

concept.body: Thirds means splitting a whole into 3 equal parts — a new share alongside halves (2 parts) and fourths (4 parts). The 3 pieces must be truly equal in size.
